result.delta_one_sentence: A builds a compression pipeline (expert pruning, routing changes and imatrix sub-2-bit quantization) so a giant MoE fits in laptop memory, and mostly compares it with other quantizations of the same model; B builds no compressor and instead uses a preregistered asymmetric test of whether an unpruned, streamed sub-2-bit giant beats smaller resident models from other families under the same memory ceiling.
result.reasoning:
Different mechanisms. A is a method and artifact paper: it stacks three known techniques (activation-guided expert pruning, top-k and routing adjustment, importance-matrix mixed-precision PTQ) to produce a resident ~100 GB model, and its claim is about deployability plus relative quality. B is an evaluation and decision study: it changes nothing in the model, accepts streaming, and asks whether a giant's parameter surplus survives sub-2-bit quantization well enough to justify a ~20x decode penalty. They share only the setting: a giant MoE, sub-2-bit PTQ and a consumer memory limit.

Why B is stronger. (1) A's main baselines are self-referential. Uniform 1-bit and 2-bit quantizations of the same model at 140 GB and 230 GB do not fit the 128 GB limit, so the comparison never tests the question a practitioner faces: is this better than a smaller model that fits natively? B makes exactly that comparison the core of its design, matching by eligibility on the same machine. (2) A's cross-family comparison is not controlled. The 210 GB reasoning variant also exceeds the 128 GB laptop, sizes differ (210 vs 233 GB), and "equal or higher on three benchmarks" has no confidence intervals or margin. (3) A uses standard, contamination-prone MC, commonsense and GSM-style benchmarks, with no reported sampling or seed control and no uncertainty. B has frozen items, three seeds, a non-contestant judge audited against blind hand labels, benchmarks with opposite contamination exposure, multiplicity-adjusted bounds, a 5-point practical margin, an intersection-union test for the win claim, and a compute-matched reasoning-budget check. Every outcome maps to a deployment decision, so a negative result is informative too. (4) A's novelty is low, since each step is known and the contribution is mostly their combination and an engineering result (>5 tok/s at ~100 GB).

Caveats against B. It contributes no new mechanism. Its scope is narrow (short-answer factual recall, non-reasoning mode). Its results bear on one giant and one machine class. And it runs everything on server GPUs, so the speed tiers are asserted rather than measured end to end. Even so, its design yields a falsifiable, decision-relevant finding, while A's evaluation cannot tell whether pruning plus quantization beats simply running a smaller model.

Feasibility.lens: Feasibility: is the pilot decisive, can it run on about 3 free H100s within 8 GPU-h before 2026-10-20 while Kimi needs about 4, and is the full study affordable and does it change a decision?
Feasibility.strongest_argument:
The pilot can probably run. What fails is that it is decisive only in the direction that changes nothing Kevin does, and a large part of the full study measures configurations the proposal itself calls unusable.

(1) The deployment decision is predetermined. In the registration's own table (section 7.3), Kevin's local model is a resident model under NOT_WORTH, under LEADS_INSTANT_ONLY or LEADS_PROVISIONAL, and under UNRESOLVED, SPLIT or UNRESOLVED_INCOMPLETE, where the table says "Unchanged". Only a full LEADS that also passes H5 changes the choice.

(2) That branch is structurally underpowered within 8 GPU-h.
- LEADS needs all four contrasts at 1,000 or more items, and then P2 out of the 1.1 GPU-h reserve.
- P2's own estimate is 0.46-2.65 GPU-h against a 0.7 guard. With about 1,000 thinking tokens per item it needs about 1.2 GPU-h, so it gets cut at roughly half its items.
- H5 has no coverage minimum, unlike KC4. It is a single-seed test on at most 600 items. The SE is about 2.1-2.3 points at full coverage, about 3 at 300 items, and about 5 at the pessimistic 125.
- 2603.09906 (Google, Thinking to Recall) shows that reasoning raises single-hop SimpleQA-Verified pass@1. Even a dummy trace lifts Gemini-2.5-Flash from 0.206 to 0.262. A resident model that thinks should therefore erase an instant-mode lead near the 5-point margin. A true lead of 8 points in instant mode passes H5 with only about 0.3 probability even at full coverage.
- With the desk forecast's P(LEADS) ≈ 0.15 before H5, the chance that the pilot changes Kevin's local model is about 0.1 or less.

(3) The decision it does make, dropping Kimi from the full study, is deferred. NOT_WORTH on the deprecated K2.5 still requires a K2.6 IQ1_M confirmation run "because K2.6 is the Kimi a user would stream today". That 232.4 GB file is about a 15-30 minute CPU-lane fetch at the 290 MB/s the host prep measured. The decisive model could simply be the pilot's Kimi arm.

(4) The full study's UNRESOLVED and LEADS branches budget K2.6 IQ1_M in the thinking tier.
- That is 18.85M tokens per arm, 46.5-139.6 GPU-h, plus 34-251 GPU-h for the INT4 reference.
- At 2.2 tok/s on the Mac, 14K-token math traces take about 106 minutes per item. The proposal excludes Kimi thinking from the pilot for exactly this reason: it "would match no usable Mac configuration".
- So this spend cannot change a deployment decision.
- The NOT_WORTH branch (112-249 GPU-h) has no Kimi arm except the confirmation run. It is a resident-model and G4 study under LM1's name.

(5) The guards were set before the parallel-slot throughput pilot D127 asked for. The caps file's "pessimistic" Kimi prefill, 600 tok/s, is above the only measurement, 411 tok/s. In that regime, top-ups for Kimi and gpt-oss consume the reserve and P2 cannot run, so the pilot is one-sided by arithmetic as well as by design.
Feasibility.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any one of these, ideally together:

(a) A measured parallel-slot throughput preflight (the throughput pilot D127 asked for) for Kimi at K3 or K3+ and for gpt-oss at low effort. It would need to show that all 1,600 primary items finish inside the guards and still leave the 0.7 GPU-h P2 reserve intact.

(b) An H5 power analysis with a minimum coverage rule. Alternatively, make the free majority-of-three estimand, or a fully funded P2, the input to the decision. Either way, show that a true Kimi lead of 8 points survives a resident model that thinks with probability 0.8 or more.

(c) A decision table in which at least one likely reading changes Kevin's local model, or a showing that dropping Kimi from the full study is worth at least the pilot's 8 GPU-h without the K2.6 confirmation.

(d) Removing the Kimi K2.6 thinking-tier arms (46.5-139.6 GPU-h) from the full study's UNRESOLVED and LEADS branches, which would match the pilot's own exclusion. Or replacing them with Mac-time-matched Kimi budgets, costed as such.

(e) Running K2.6 IQ1_M as the pilot's Kimi arm after Kevin's go-ahead for the roughly 30-minute fetch, so that NOT_WORTH is final rather than deferred.

Identification.lens: Identification. Can the pilot attribute a quality difference to the choice of model and bit-width, given confounds such as reasoning mode and token budget, sampler, chat template, CUDA versus Metal numerics, benchmark choice and contamination? And do its outcomes measure what it claims? I read the proposal, the draft registration lm1-matched-memory-quality-v1, sim_lm1.py, the LM1 host-prep README, the dossier, and the G2 proposal's Anemll section, all on branch gauntlet/lm1-matched-memory-quality at 9008efc2. I edited nothing.
Identification.strongest_argument:
The pilot's most likely reading is NOT_WORTH (desk forecast 0.55). That reading cannot be attributed to the 1.87-bit choice, and the primary endpoint does not measure the edge the design is built on.

(1) Half of the endpoint already has a large gap at full precision, and the pilot has no Kimi reference to separate model from bits.
- Epoch AI's independent result, at full precision, puts Kimi K2.5 at 34% on SimpleQA Verified.
- The registration's own sources give Qwen3-235B-2507 54.3 on SimpleQA (vendor number; Kimi K2 31.0).
- With equal benchmark weights, that gap adds about -10 points to Δ_Q before quantization enters at all. If the published numbers carry over, Kimi would need about a +25-point lead over Qwen on AA-Omniscience just to avoid NOT_WORTH (Bonferroni upper bound of about Δ̂ + 2.6 against the +5 margin).
- A higher-precision Kimi (INT4) appears only in the full study's LEADS branch. So the pilot cannot tell "1.87 bits destroyed recall" apart from "K2.5 never matched Qwen on SimpleQA", or from Qwen's unexplained jump from 12.2 to 54.3, which the proposal itself flags as exposure that would favour Qwen.
- The registration nonetheless reads KIMI_WORSE as "knowledge loss below 2 bits on a 1T MoE" and closes G3 "by dominance". Both claims are attributions to bit-width that the design cannot identify.
- The contamination guard does not protect NOT_WORTH. SPLIT fires only if AA-Omniscience alone reads a full LEADS against all four resident arms. In sim_lm1.py Kimi is the best resident arm plus the same Δ on both benchmarks, and the arms keep one ranking on both. The simulation therefore never covers opposite-sign effects per benchmark, which is the configuration the vendor numbers predict.
- The precedence between NOT_WORTH and SPLIT is written only in the simulation code (nw_final = not_worth & ~split), not in registration 7.3.

(2) The endpoint mixes stored knowledge with each model's willingness to abstain.
- Both benchmarks use AA's prompt, which invites abstention. NOT_WORTH uses accuracy alone; the Omniscience-index condition guards only LEADS.
- In the SimpleQA paper, Claude-3.5-Sonnet was more accurate than GPT-4o on the questions it attempted (44.5 vs 38.0) yet scored 9.3 points lower overall (28.9 vs 38.2), because it declined 35.0% of questions.
- So abstention habits alone can move accuracy by more than the 5-point margin, in the direction opposite to knowledge. Those habits differ by model family and are plausibly changed by quantization.
- A better-calibrated Kimi therefore reads NOT_WORTH or KIMI_WORSE for reasons that have nothing to do with the knowledge it has stored.

(3) The premise does not match what is tested.
- The "full-precision knowledge edge" (AA +19) is the Omniscience Index for K2.6 (Reasoning) against V4 Flash 0731 (Max). The AA page shows no accuracy values for either.
- The pilot tests K2.5 accuracy in instant mode: a different model, mode and metric.
- GSQ Table 3 (the proposal's C06) shows Kimi at about 2 bits keeping LCB, MATH500 and AIME25 but losing 12.7 points of GPQA-Diamond. Knowledge is where low-bit Kimi is damaged most, not its best case.
- So a knowledge NOT_WORTH does not license removing Kimi from the full study's reasoning and coding tier (section 18). That also contradicts section 2, which says the pilot does not decide reasoning, coding or tool use.

(4) Further confounds, all left unbounded in the pilot.
- Samplers differ by arm, and each item is scored as the share of three sampled seeds graded correct. F2, F3 and O run at T=1.0 untruncated; K at 0.6/0.95; Q at 0.7/0.8 with top-k 20. There is no greedy sensitivity run.
- That matters because ds4 Q2 matches BF16's top token only 78.98% of the time (C29), so untruncated sampling adds quantization noise unequally across arms.
- The judge: AA chose Gemini 2.5 Flash with reasoning over Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking and gpt-oss-120b because it agreed better with human grading. The pilot uses a smaller Qwen3-32B, from the same family as arm Q, with thinking off and 4 output tokens.
- The judge check uses agent labels on 72 items per arm. A Rogan-Gladen correction at that size has a standard error of roughly 3 points per arm, so the judge gate either voids the reading or cannot detect bias between arms.
- Mac transfer: the Mac speed cited for Kimi (2.2 tokens/s) comes from Anemll's CPU path (-ngl 0 -ub 1). Its Metal path showed "degraded output on some runs". The host runs everything in VRAM under CUDA.
- The dossier records a 4-5% perplexity difference between two CUDA kernel paths on the same BF16 file. Every kernel-path check is deferred to the full study, which runs only after the pilot has already decided.
Identification.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any one of the following would weaken the refutation; all of them together would overturn it.
- **A Kimi reference:** a higher-precision Kimi arm on the same harness, at least on a subset (K2.5 INT4 or Q4 by CPU offload of experts into the host's 1.77 TB RAM, or after 2026-10-20). Otherwise, drop every bit-width attribution (the KIMI_WORSE "knowledge loss below 2 bits" reading and G3 "closes by dominance").
- **Primary endpoint:** AA-Omniscience alone as primary, or a per-benchmark rule with the NOT_WORTH/SPLIT precedence stated in 7.3. Plus a simulation in which the arm ranking and the sign of Δ differ between the benchmarks.
- **Abstention control:** a forced-answer prompt (no abstention line), or a NOT_WORTH rule that also requires Kimi to trail on accuracy among attempted questions and on the index.
- **Samplers:** a greedy sensitivity run across all arms.
- **Judge:** one from outside the arms' families, or AA's grader, validated against human labels at a size where the per-arm correction is precise to about 1 point.
- **Host evidence:** a measurement showing Qwen Q3_K_XL's SimpleQA-Verified accuracy under this prompt is within a few points of Kimi's, so the gap in model identity does not predetermine the reading.
- **Scope:** section 18 revised so that a knowledge-only NOT_WORTH no longer removes Kimi from the reasoning and coding tier.

Novelty.strongest_argument:

Someone has already compared a giant at about 1.8 bits per weight with the best models that fit a 128 GB tier, across model families, on a knowledge-weighted task.

oobabooga's benchmark table is sorted by file size. It uses 48 private multiple-choice questions on "academic knowledge and logical reasoning", and the page was last updated 2026-01-08 (community source, first-party). It lists:
- DeepSeek-V3 i1-IQ1_M (671B, 148.9 GB, about 1.78 bpw; on a 128 GB Mac this file would have to stream) at 23/48;
- Qwen3-235B i1-IQ3_XS / IQ3_S / IQ3_M (96.0-103.1 GB, LM1's R-T tier) at 40/48;
- Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 UD-Q2_K_XL (88.8 GB, LM1's own Qwen arm at a smaller file) at 39/48;

- Unsloth's Aider page compares DeepSeek-V3.1 at TQ1_0 (170 GB) with full-precision Qwen3-235B.

The knowledge-capacity premise is also published. IKP (2604.24827) finds that factual recall is log-linear in parameter count across 93 open models from 135M to 1.6T, Kimi K2.5 included. The proposal read only its abstract and does not cite it.

synthesis_result.closest_prior_mechanism_paragraph: To deploy an ultra-large mixture-of-experts language model (several hundred billion parameters) on an edge laptop with a strict 128 GB memory limit, combine three compression steps: expert pruning that removes about a quarter of the experts in each layer, guided by activation statistics on calibration data; activation adjustments that reduce the number of experts used per token and suppress routing to removed experts; and mixed-precision post-training quantization at an average below 2 bits per weight, allocated with an importance matrix. The result is a model of about 100 GB that runs at over 5 tokens per second on the laptop. Its quality is compared with uniform low-bit quantizations of the same model (a 1-bit variant at 140 GB and a 2-bit variant at 230 GB) on standard multiple-choice, commonsense and grade-school math benchmarks, where the compressed model is more accurate than the uniform 1-bit version and close to the 2-bit one at about half its size. In one further comparison, a reasoning variant of the same large model compressed to about 210 GB is compared on three reasoning benchmarks with a 235-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model from another family stored at 8 bits (about 233 GB), and it scores equal or higher on each.

synthesis_result.mechanism_paragraph: Under a fixed resident-memory ceiling on one consumer machine, compare deployable configurations of large language models on short-answer factual recall. One configuration is a very large sparse mixture-of-experts model (about a trillion parameters) post-training quantized to under 2 bits per weight; its file is about twice the memory ceiling, so on the target machine it can only run by streaming expert weights from local storage, at roughly a twentieth of the resident models' decode speed. The others are smaller models from three different families that stay resident at 2 to 4.5 bits per weight. Matching is by eligibility, not by file size: every configuration must run on the same machine within the same resident ceiling, and each is labelled by tier (fits, tight, streamed). All configurations are run on server GPUs in one fixed non-reasoning mode with each vendor's recommended sampling, on the same frozen items with three seeded samples per item, and graded by a fixed judge model that is not a contestant, audited against blind hand labels. The decision rule is asymmetric. The giant is declared not worth its speed cost if, for any resident model, the multiplicity-adjusted upper confidence bound of its accuracy advantage is below a 5-point practical margin. It is declared better only if it beats every resident model (an intersection-union test) by at least that margin, on two benchmarks whose contamination exposure runs in opposite directions. A conditional check gives the best resident model a reasoning budget equal to the tokens it can decode in the wall-clock time the streamed giant needs per item. The study tests whether the giant's parameter surplus, which should favour factual recall, survives sub-2-bit quantization, and it maps each reading to which model to run locally.
